job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Omar Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around 8, make coffee and open my laptop in the corner of the flat I share with two others. I work as a junior data analyst at a small payments startup. I studied economics and marketing, so I'm the person who builds the weekly sales dashboards and cleans messy exports. I use AI to write queries and check my formulas all day. At night I build dashboards for a couple of local shops for cash, because the loan doesn't care that my salary is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but it's still useful. Even a plateau tool saves me an hour on a bad spreadsheet. I'd tell friends to use it for the boring parts and not expect miracles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my situation doesn't change much, which is the problem. I'm on a low entry salary, the startup has eighteen months of money left, and nobody knows if I'd keep my job if the next funding round fails. My loan payment is more than my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my side income. I have two shop clients paying 150 a month each, and I'd try for two more. I'd also keep using AI to be faster than the senior analyst, because that's my edge. And I'd put anything extra on the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. Restless, though. I like what I'm doing, but I hate that the startup's cash could vanish in one bad quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the startup could run out of money. How do you plan around that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By having a second income so I can survive a month without a salary. I keep a list of other startups hiring analysts, and I update my portfolio every Sunday. I'm not scared of change, I'm scared of being unprepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about the pay gap between you and the founders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's unfair, honestly. I'm cleaning their data and they hold the shares. I'd like to see profit-sharing or more transparent pay. I don't say that at work, because the founders are friendly and I don't want to be 'that person' yet.

say: Even a plateau tool saves me an **hour** on a messy spreadsheet.
I'd tell friends to use AI for the **boring parts** and not expect miracles.
think: The startup has about **eighteen months** of money, and my job rides on the next round.
My **loan payment** is bigger than my rent.
do: Grow my side income by adding **two more** shop dashboard clients.
Use AI daily to be **faster** than the senior analyst, and put extra cash on the loan.
feel: Mostly **okay**, but restless about how fast the startup's cash could vanish.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of change, I'm scared of being unprepared.
fieldNote: Adaptive: builds a **second income** rather than waiting for stability.
Keeps quiet at work about pay fairness, a gap between **say and think**.
Mood is uneasy because his own job looks safe, but the employer is shaky.

steps.text: Sign two more local shops for monthly dashboard work
Put 100 extra on the student loan each month
Use AI to rewrite slow queries and teach the team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already happening and people should get on with learning it. For my kind of work, writing queries, cleaning data and building reports, AI takes about half the hours. I'd tell friends in finance to stop pretending it's a toy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I think I'm in the first wave. If one analyst with AI does the work of two, the startup hires one of us, not two. I'm junior, so I'm a candidate for the one who goes. But I'm also the one who knows the tools best, so I could be the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who runs the AI workflows for the whole team and make that visible: write a short guide, show the CEO a dashboard that took 20 minutes instead of two days. And I'd widen the side clients and consider freelancing full-time if pay doesn't rise. I'd also ask for a pay review in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous in equal parts. It's like surfing, which I've never done, but I imagine you have to keep moving or you go under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company doesn't see your value?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I leave. I've already saved the names of three other startups and two agencies. I'd rather work somewhere that sees a junior analyst with AI as a bargain than somewhere that sees me as a cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Beatriz, who does data entry at a logistics firm. She's brilliant but refuses to learn the new tools. I keep saying to her, just try it for twenty minutes. She says it's not her job to train the machine. I think it's going to hurt her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public action right now, because it's not going to be fair by default. Two years is too short for companies to be left to decide. I'd post about it, sign petitions and push my MP for a basic income and a ban on firing without notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the scariest one. If AI can do almost any thinking work, my edge, being good with AI tools, disappears because everyone, including the CEO, can do it. I'd be a junior analyst with no savings and a loan. I really don't see where I'd stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for work that requires being physically present. I've been thinking about taking a short electrician or heat pump course, even though I know robots come later. I'd spend as little as possible and build a six-month buffer by selling my second monitor and my bike. I'd also go to meetings about income support and unions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stomach-drop scared. I've told myself I'm adaptable and now I'm not sure that means anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being good with AI tools stops being an edge. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone can talk to a machine and get a finished analysis, what am I selling? I'm 22, I have a pass degree, and no famous employer. The edge goes to whoever owns something, not to whoever uses it well. That's what hits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the trade idea feel like yours, or something you reach for out of panic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. I like making things work, so I'd probably enjoy it. But it feels like running to a boat that's leaving three years after the one I'm on. I'd rather it exists as a bridge than a destination.

say: Two years is too short to leave this to **companies**.
I'd push my MP for a **basic income** and no firing without notice.
think: If everyone can use AI, my **edge disappears** and I'm a junior with a loan.
The value goes to **owners**, not users.
do: Start a short **electrician or heat pump** course for work that needs presence.
Build a **six-month buffer** by selling my second monitor and bike.
feel: **Stomach-drop scared**, and unsure whether being adaptable still means anything.
S2.quote: The edge goes to whoever owns something, not to whoever uses it well.
fieldNote: Even the most AI-fluent of the nine sees his **edge vanish** in two years.
Trade idea is part interest, part **panic**, and he says both.
Expects to lose his job and has no savings, so **alarmed**.

steps.text: Sign up for a short heat pump installer course
Sell my second monitor and bike to start a buffer
Email my MP about a basic income and notice rules
Go to an income-support campaign meeting each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to organise but short enough that we shouldn't wait. I'd go on about transitions and who gets the profits. I'd tell friends to keep a side income and learn what the new tools can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a race. I'd be 27 and I could be one of the people who built a small business around AI services before it gets crowded. Or I could be another analyst whose job disappeared the year before AGI. It depends on what I do in the next two years, and that's quite motivating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd focus on turning my side work into a small agency that sells data and automation help to small shops. Year one, I'd aim for six clients. I'd keep the job for stability, keep the cost of living low and pay off the high-interest loan first. I'd save enough for six months before leaving anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Charged up. The deadline is scary but it gives me something to build towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would small shops pay you if AGI is coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd pay for someone they know to explain it and set it up, because they don't trust an anonymous tool. I'd be the local person with a face. That's valuable for a few years at least, though I wouldn't expect it to last past the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the agency isn't enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd switch to something that runs on trust and presence, maybe teaching or training others on the tools. Anything but wait. Waiting's the thing I'm worst at.

I'd tell friends to keep a **side income** and learn what the tools can't do.

steps.text: Package dashboard and automation help for small shops as a service

Spend 200 on a legal set-up and simple website

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and it's a waste if we just argue about it. I'd push for retraining funds and make sure the benefits are shared. I'd be telling friends to treat it like a long project: study, save, experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel optimistic with some guilt. I could have a decade of building experience, savings and a real business, maybe one that employs a few people. But I'd feel guilty about the people who don't have my tools, like Beatriz and my cousin, who left school at 16.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for a couple of years to clear most of my loan, then go freelance or start something. I'd study part-time for a master's in data science, which I couldn't afford now. I'd help Beatriz learn the tools and I'd save for a deposit. I'd also give some time to a community project teaching AI basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. It's the first one where I can see myself at 30 with a plan and some choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the guilt come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I got lucky with a flatmate who showed me the tools and a degree that, even though it was just a pass, lets me stay in the room. A lot of people don't have either. It feels odd to say I'm fine while they're not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might go wrong in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Complacency. I could get comfortable at a decent salary and stop pushing. Or the startup collapses and I spend two years stuck. But ten years lets me recover from a mistake, which the others don't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My whole plan assumes my skills are worth something, and in two years they might not be. What would help is a real safety net for the first year, something like a basic income, and employers who share what they save. For me personally, a free retraining place and a cheap place to live for a year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That I'm not an AI cheerleader. I use it because I have to eat. If the people who own the machines don't share the gains, I'm just a well-trained employee for a shorter time.

headlineQuote: I'm not an AI cheerleader. I use it because I have to eat.
portrait: Omar is a **22-year-old** junior data analyst at a payments startup with a heavy loan and almost no savings.
He uses AI every day, builds shop dashboards on the side, and sees tools as his **bargaining chip**.
He leans left, points at **owners and profit-sharing**, and wants public support.
He moves early in every scenario: side clients, a fallback employer list, a study plan.
His mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** in the two-year case, when he fears his edge disappears.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his skills could stop being worth anything while he has a loan and no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** for the first year, shared gains from employers, free retraining and cheap housing.
